Next, I moved on to the 2-pc Chicken Wing (S$4) . These absolutely stole the spotlight for me, hitting every mark of what a great fried chicken wing should be. Marinated in yoghurt, the meat stayed wonderfully tender and juicy on the inside.
Outside, the crust boasted a super crispy finish packed with savoury seasoning. Honestly, it was a masterclass in fried chicken wings — flavourful enough that you don’t even need the accompanying chilli sauce.
Who is Charr’d The Hawker best for?
If you’re looking for a comforting, old-school Western-style meal with generous and thoughtfully executed sides, Charr’d The Hawker is well worth a visit. The chefs’ fine-dining background shines through in the little details, elevating familiar hawker staples like the vibrant, crunchy coleslaw. It’s an easy go-to for Muslim diners and groups hunting for hearty and affordable Western fare in the Beach Road area.
How to get to Charr’d The Hawker
Charr’d The Hawker is located on the basement level of Golden Mile Food Centre, which is a quick 7-minute walk from Nicoll Highway MRT Station . The station connects to the MRT Circle Line. Take Exit A and walk along Java Road before turning left onto Beach Road.
If you prefer to travel by bus, alight at Opp St. John HQ (01411) or St. John HQ (01419) along Beach Road. Do note that bus service 961M operates exclusively on Sundays and public holidays, while all other bus services operate daily.
Do we recommend Charr’d The Hawker?
Yes! I thoroughly enjoyed every element of the plate as each felt intentional and was done well. That said, on my next visit, I would opt for the chicken wing set instead of the chicken chop. While the chicken chop had a great crust, the fillet was slightly on the thinner side, whereas the wings were easily the star of the meal.

BAO Fast Foods (BFF) is a new concept from London’s cult-favourite BAO . After a homecoming run in Taiwan, the pop-up will next land in Singapore at New Bahru from 11 November 2026 to 28 December 2026 .
But what exactly is this experience that is part fast food joint , part Asian convenience store ? Keep reading to find out more!
Credit: BAO
For those of you who enjoy exploring convenience stores when you’re overseas, especially in Asian countries like Taiwan, you will find the vibes here immaculate. At BFF, there will be a sense of familiarity with a distinct Taiwan flavour.
Credit: BAO
Expect shelves filled with Taiwanese comfort food and snacks , and a rotating selection of grab-and-go items. There will also be self-serve stations and sections featuring BAO’s merchandise .
From protein-packed bites like Egg Sandos and Marinated Eggs to high-fibre sides like “Fried Rice” Quinoa and Golden Kimchi , to sweet treats like Soy Puddings with tiramisu and banoffee toppings, you’ll have plenty to discover and revisit the pop-up for.
Credit: BAO
The signature item, however, is the Chicken Chopper (S$6.50) . Of course, when it comes to Taiwanese snacks, you must have fried chicken . And this is BFF’s take on the classic street food, perfected over 140 iterations.
You will notice that the chicken is cut with the bone left in place as a handle, making it easy to eat. By dipping the chicken in a soymilk batter and coating it in a tapioca starch mix, BFF ensures the meat stays juicy while having a light, crackly crust on the outside.
Flavours to look forward to include Original Crispy , Flame Glazed , and Master Scalded . The first is seasoned with Taiwanese white pepper, the second is flavoured with soy-garlic or mala hot honey glaze, and the third is dipped in a boiling soy-based master sauce with star anise and cinnamon.
Credit: BAO
For a more filling meal, you can order the Chicken Chopper as part of a rice box (S$7.95) , or pair it with Dan Dan Noodles (S$6.50) or Beef Cup Noodle (S$12.50) . Combos from S$9.50 are also available.
Credit: BAO
Another staple of Taiwanese food culture is tea ! And you will be able to find a selection of Taiwanese craft tea here at the BFF pop-up. Highlights include the nitro-infused Fluffy Natural Alishan Wintermelon (S$5.95) , the carbonated Orange Guava Beauty Tea (S$6.50) , and the rich Original Peanut Oatside Milk (S$6) .
If anything about this pop-up excites you, mark your calendars from 11 November to 28 December. It’s time to have a date at the convenience store!

World Christmas Market returns from 10 December 2026
Image credit: World Christmas Market
PSA: The Christmas market that drew more than 218,000 people to Marina Bay last year is moving house. World Christmas Market is back for a third edition, now called A Christmas Story by World Christmas Market . It runs from 10 December 2026 to 3 January 2027 on the grounds of METT Hotel Singapore and Fort Canning Park . Even better, entry is free for everyone.
We Visited World Christmas Market 2025, A Festive Fair At Bayfront With Over 40 Stalls
The fair started in 2024 at The Promontory at Marina Bay. In 2025, it moved to the much bigger Bayfront Event Space as Togetherland by World Christmas Market .
We went last year and counted over 40 food and drink stalls, from Rollney’s ice cream-stuffed chimney cakes to chilled and grilled oysters at Slurp Your Oysters.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
This year the organisers, DareDreamer, are swapping the waterfront for something greener and more old-school, with the fair spread across the hilltop park and the grounds of the colonial-era hotel.
The fair is split into three zones. The first, The Story Terrace, has festive shopping, gifts, and hands-on workshops. It’s also home to The Long Table, a communal dining setup where you can share a meal with friends or end up chatting with strangers.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
Next is The Piazza, the main square. A 38-foot real Christmas tree stands in the middle, with smaller decorated trees all around it. The third zone, The Merry Grounds, is where the food is. Expect seasonal bites, festive drinks, and plenty of reasons to stick around. If you’re mainly going to eat, start here. The full vendor lineup is still TBD, since the festival is still taking applications from F&B, retail, and craft vendors. We’ll update this article once the stalls are confirmed.
Across the grounds, look out for giant nutcrackers and glowing reindeer, which make good photo backdrops. There’s plenty of music too. A 42-piece orchestra plays on opening weekend. Brass sextets, saxophone quartets, and choirs perform on other dates throughout the season.
Image credit: World Christmas Market
On opening night, 10 December 2026, the gates open at 5pm. The tree-lighting and opening ceremony starts at 7.30pm, so arrive early for a good spot. The fair also stays open until 1am on Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve, so it works for a late-night date or a countdown with friends.

The vibes here are luxurious yet casual. And the menu? Distinctively local and halal-sourced . I don’t visit Muslim-friendly hotpot restaurants that often, so I wasn’t exactly sure what to expect. But let’s just say that after having lunch here, I’m definitely coming back if I get the chance!
The Kopitiam Classics
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
The concept at JING Halal Hotpot & Grill Buffet is simple: each diner gets their own individual hotpot , while every table has a shared grill . Buffet lunch prices for adults start at S$41.90++ on weekdays and from S$47.90++ on weekends . All-you-can-eat dinner prices start at S$47.9++ .
During our weekday lunch at JING, we tried signature menu items themed around ‘ Kopitiam Classics ’ On The Grill , such as Housemade Otah , Hainanese Chicken , and Salted Egg Prawns . My personal recommendation would be the Salted Egg Prawns, which had freshness and flavour that kept me going back for seconds.
Hotpot Broths
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
We also opted for hotpot broths with strong local inspiration – Laksa and Prawn Mee . These flavours might be too rich and savoury for some, but I never felt it was too much for me. I especially loved the Prawn Mee broth, which worked really well with the hotpot ingredients, adding umami goodness to every bite and sip.
Range of Ingredients
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
Speaking of hotpot ingredients, there is quite a wide range to choose from here, especially for meat lovers. Marinated House Specialities include Goji Berry Chicken , Sarawak Black Pepper Beef , Beef Mala , Tom Yum Chicken , and more.
Seafood such as Tiger Prawns , Freshwater Patin Fish , and Black Mussels are also available. Cook your ingredients in your soup of choice or throw them on the grill – it’s up to you how you want to enjoy your meal.
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
There are also ready-to-eat items at one of the counters. Do yourself a favour and get some of these fried mantou with chilli crab sauce . There’s nothing better to have while waiting for your other ingredients to finish cooking.
Desserts
Photo by Soh Zhen Wei (Confirm Good)
Another honourable mention under The Kopitiam Classics menu is the Bubur Pulut Hitam . Yes, desserts are available! And we devoured a bowl of these so quickly. The warm black glutinous rice and coconut cream combination has just the right sweetness and texture that leaves you wanting more.
The Lucky Roll

If the food at JING hasn’t convinced you to visit yet, this probably will. From now to 30 December 2026 , groups of 3–6 pax can participate in The Lucky Roll and stand a chance to win an entire meal on the restaurant’s tab.

Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee is a nearly 4-decade-old Michelin-recognised institution which has been serving handmade fishballs and Teochew-style noodles in Pasar 16 @ Bedok . For any foodies hunting down old-school hawker fare in the East, this stall is a must-visit for the decades of heritage it brings to the table.
As rare as handmade fishballs are, handmade fishballs made from ikan parang are even harder to come across. I kan parang is bony and difficult to process into fishballs and most stalls use yellowtail instead. Stepping up to a stall that goes the extra mile immediately had me excited to try their fare.
What to order at Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee
I opted for Dry Fishball Noodles with Mee Pok (S$4) to enjoy at the hawker centre, and got the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow (S$4) along with an extra side of Fishball Soup (S$7) to-go.
One serving of Dry Fishball Noodles gets you a generous portion of your noodles of choice, a bowl of clear soup containing 5 precious fishballs and 1 her giao , a traditional Teochew fish dumpling.
The fishballs are definitely the highlight for me. They possess a satisfying bounce and irregular shaping, all telltale signs of a handmade fishball. They possess a naturally sweet flavour from the flesh of ikan parang , and you can tell that not much filler is used as the fishballs don’t have that flour-heavy, starchy bite that commercial surimi fishballs are often guilty of.
When bitten, it breaks apart in tender layers of flesh. It’s quite minimally seasoned so the flavour of the fresh fish meat really shines through. The her giao differs texturally with a firmer, chewier texture and is distinctly less sweet than the fishballs.
The soup was similarly lightly seasoned and contained bits of preserved vegetables which gave it a slight salty finish, which complemented the subtle sweetness of the fishballs well.
Mei Ling Fishball Noodle Showdown: Xin Lu Teochew Fishball Noodles vs Hup Kee Teochew Fishball Noodles
Unfortunately, the mee pok noodles were a little disappointing. I opted for the spicy version, which had the perfect kick and a good balance of sweet and savoury. Sadly, the noodles were quite alkaline-tasting and the sauce didn’t cling but had a clumpy, gummy texture. On the bright side, it was an extremely generous portion and quite filling.
If I came back, I’d recommend either skipping or getting a small portion of noodles and filling up on more fishballs.
As for the Fishball Noodle Soup with Kway Teow , it features the same amount of handmade fishballs and her giao as the dry version, but with flat, white rice noodles in the soup instead.
Disclaimer: If the fishballs look extra plentiful in this photo, that’s because I combined the noodles with the S $7 Fishball Soup, which comes with more fishballs and her giao than the standard S$ 4 bowl!
As I had them to-go, the noodles had soaked up the soup by the time I got home and became quite soft, easily breaking apart when I held them up with chopsticks. Texturally, it wasn’t too bad and was able to retain some chew despite the long journey home.
Who is Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee best for?
I can imagine Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee being best for handmade fishball purists who appreciate labour-intensive ikan parang fishballs. With how rare such fishballs are, I’d highly recommend this stall to anyone looking to try the real deal before it disappears from the hawker scene entirely. The stall is also ideal for those with larger appetites who prefer generous portions of filling noodles.
How to get to Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee
Hock Seng Choon Fish Ball Kway Teow Mee is located within Pasar 16 @ Bedok, which is a 15-minute walk from Bedok MRT Station (EW5) . The station connects to the MRT East-West (Green) Line.
Alternatively, take bus service 31 or 137 from Bedok Stn Exit A (84039) and alight at Fujitech S’pore Ltd (84129) and walk 7 min down Bedok South Road towards Pasar 16 @ Bedok. You can also alight at Blk 18 (84119) or Opp Blk 17 (84111) and walk 3 min towards Pasar 16 @ Bedok.
Do we recommend Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee?
Overall, I’d recommend Hock Seng Choon Fishball Kway Teow Mee purely for the handmade ikan parang fishballs — after almost 40 years, they remain the undeniable star of the stall. While the noodles may have been slightly below expectations, you can easily work around this by skipping the noodles altogether or ordering a small portion and loading up on extra fishballs instead.

It’s the end of an era for Assam laksa lovers. Popular regional chain D’Laksa is officially winding down operations, pulling out of Singapore after almost 10 years of serving up its signature tangy mackerel-packed Assam laksa . As a farewell treat, D’Laksa is also running a Buy-2-Get-1-Free promotion at its last outlet at Compass One before permanently shuttering on 23 Nov 2026 .
Originally hailing from Johor Bahru, D’Laksa was known for offering the less common Penang-style laksa, which forgoes the more usual coconut milk base in favour of a robust, spicy fish-based broth. The brand built a loyal following through its quick-service kiosks nestled inside neighbourhood malls and food courts (including past spots like YewTee Point and Northpoint City).
Their signature dish of Asam Laksa (S$6) comes with a generous portion of lettuce, pineapple and fish, giving the dish a tart aroma thanks to the sweet, sour and tangy flavours it packs. Their special prawn paste complements the sour tamarind sauce with its heavily umami profile. They also offer Asam Lobsterball (S$4.50) , which comes with 5 pieces of bouncy lobster balls drenched in their signature Assam sauce.
Credit – D’Laksa
Alternatively, try their Asam Pedas Stingray with Rice (S$8.90) , which features a slab of stingray meat dressed in a bold, spicy gravy. Sides and beverages such as Fruit Rojak (S$5.50) and Cendol Drink (S$2.50) are also available.
While the brand has steadily scaled back its islandwide footprint over recent months, this quiet closure marks the end of D’Laksa in Singapore, with only their Johor Bahru outlets remaining. Fans of D’Laksa should head down to Compass One before 23 Nov to enjoy the Buy-2-Get-1-Free deal and get one last bowl of their favourite Penang-style Assam Laksa; otherwise, you’ll have to trek across the border to get a taste.

We all know and love Orchard Road as an iconic shopping destination in Singapore. But when the hunger pangs call, finding the perfect dining spot can leave us stumped – especially if you’re searching for a quiet restaurant away from the crowds that delivers on its ambience, food and drinks. Enter Slainte at Paragon, Orchard, a newly revamped sanctuary that hits all the marks. Made for intimate date nights and convivial group hangouts alike, Slainte might be that day-to-night spot you need on your radar.
Slainte at Orchard: Details at a glance
Best for: An inviting day-to-night spot with charcoal-grilled dishes and rare whiskies
Must-try dishes: Snow aging yukimuro full blood wagyu; miso-glazed Patagonian toothfish; salt-roasted carabinero; Iberico pluma
Price: Starters from $9; mains from $19; desserts from $19; drinks from $5
Opening hours: Daily, 11am to 10pm
Address: #04-09, Paragon Shopping Centre, 290 Orchard Road, Singapore 238859
Cosy up in a chic and inviting setting
Photography: Slainte
Step inside Slainte, and you’ll be instantly enveloped in a warm and welcoming ambience. From the cave-like stone walls to wooden furnishing and warm glow, every inch of the restaurant is designed to make you linger.
With a perfect balance of intimacy and luxury, it is a space that makes for easy and effortless conversations. Coupled with its quieter location away from the main shopping strip, Slainte is where you can finally take a breather from the hustle and bustle.
A smoky menu takes centre stage
Bold, smoky flavours and charcoal grilling anchor the menu at Slainte. The restaurant’s state-of-the-art Kopa oven is where all the grilling magic happens. Fired by charcoal and applewood, this showstopper reaches a blistering 600 degrees Celsius.
The results? An irresistible menu kissed by smoke, serving up unbeatable juiciness and deeply charred flavours that can’t be replicated at home.
Photography: Slainte
The flame-grilled selection beckons with signatures like black Angus porterhouse ($78), char siew Iberico pork jowl ($17) with a sweet-savoury glaze, Jack’s Creek wagyu hanger steak ($58), miso-glazed Patagonian toothfish ($38), and an 18-hour-marinated ayam bakar ($24).
And don’t miss the Iberico pork ($42) cooked to medium-well – we hear it’s one of the best in town. Enjoy these succulent meats and seafood with moreish sides ($9 each) like French onion mac and cheese, smashed crispy potatoes and charred asparagus.
Beyond these charcoal-grilled creations, we’re also eyeing starters like the scallop and prawn tartlets ($25) for a savoury pastry with fresh seafood, and hearty plates such as the signature yuzu kosho pasta ($29). With an extensive selection of pasta, vibrant salads and hearty mains, you’ll be left happily spoilt for choice from day through night.
Sip auctioned-sourced whiskies by the dram
Photography: Slainte
Curious about the world of whisky? Take a seat at Slainte to get started. The restaurant offers a collection of auction-sourced rare whisky that you can sip by the dram from just $15. Take it as your licence to try lesser seen whisky labels, each with its unique taste, history and craftsmanship.
Wines, champagne and creative cocktails are also available. We recommend trying the specially concocted cocktails, including the signature Slainte. An ode to the restaurant’s Irish roots, it is a blend of smoky Islay Scotch, sweet vermouth, Aperol and cinnamon.
Hello Slainte, our new go-to spot in Orchard
In an area known for glitz and sky-high prices, Slainte is where you can treat yourself to a well-crafted dining experience without the hefty price tags. On your next shopping spree in Orchard, swing by the restaurant to indulge in charcoal-grilled delicacies and sip fine whiskies and cocktails.
Curious about its allure? Visit Slainte at Paragon, Orchard, and you’ll understand why it is a dining destination that makes you linger a while longer.

Base Gelato is a new gelato bar in Joo Chiat
If you’ve recently gone cafe-hopping in Joo Chiat , you’ve probably visited the usual hotspots such as Common Man Coffee Roasters and Elijah Pies . You might, however, miss an unassuming hole-in-the-wall shop that has recently opened right under everyone’s noses. Base Gelato is a new cafe in Joo Chiat by Creamier, selling specialty gelato flavours at nett prices.

The space itself is very cosy and slightly dim. It boasts an industrial look, with natural light seeping in through the glass door.
Their menu is relatively straightforward: there are only six items to choose from. Each flavour of ice cream is specially curated, paired with its own unique accompaniments.
Their signature flavour is the Joo Chiat Heritage ($10) , which pays homage to the locale’s Peranakan history. It features a scoop of refreshing young coconut gelato topped with smoked gula melaka caramel and grated coconut, served alongside a skewer of QQ, house-made ondeh ondeh dango.
For those who prefer stronger flavours, order the Rum Raisin Vanilla Panna Cotta ($12) . The base is a layer of jiggly, silky vanilla panna cotta, made from locally grown Madagascar vanilla pods. It is topped with Jamaican rum-infused gelato and chewy sun-dried Xinjiang raisins for a nice textural contrast.
As a matcha addict, my personal favourite has got to be their Matchagato ($12) .
You can expect kinako, AKA roasted soybean powder, gelato encased in a chewy mochi wrapper and topped with azuki bean paste. Matcha is then hand-whisked right in front of you and poured over the whole shebang. I was pleased to know that their matcha is sourced from Wazakura, a prominent tea-producing region from Uji known for producing matcha that tastes rich with a smooth finish.
For something on the lighter end, the Yoghurt & Honey ($10) features triple-strained Greek yoghurt gelato similar to frozen yoghurt . It is topped with toasted honey fluff and garnished with wildflower honey and locally grown edible flowers.
This was my colleague’s favourite. The gelato was creamy with a slight tang from the yoghurt, while the honey fluff was similar to meringue, adding a nice airiness and sweetness to the dessert.
Image credit: Cindy Tan via Google Maps
We didn’t get to try all of their flavours, but the Black Forest ($12) will probably be a hit among chocolate lovers . This dessert consists of a bittersweet Valrhona Coeur De Guanaja 80% chocolate gelato topped with a dollop of cream and a wild Morello cherry, served alongside a dark chocolate sponge that’s soaked in cherry-infused kirsch.
